q: Which step may safely run **before** the train/test split?
o: Removing rows with a negative monthly fee
Capping usage at the IQR upper bound
Filling missing ages with the median age
Dropping values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean
e: A fixed domain rule does not learn anything from the data. IQR bounds, medians and z-scores are computed from rows, so they must come from the training set only.

q: What is the difference between an invalid value and an outlier?
o: There is none; both should be removed
Outliers are always typos, invalid values are real
An invalid value is impossible (age 211); an outlier is possible but extreme (a very heavy user)
Invalid values are nulls, outliers are non-null
e: Fix or remove impossible values with rules. Investigate outliers before you decide, because they may carry signal.

o: Rows with at most 8 null values
Rows with at least 8 non-null values
The first 8 columns
Columns with fewer than 8 nulls
e: `thresh` is the minimum number of non-null values a row needs to be kept. It overrides `how`.

q: A few values are 10 times too large. Why does the z-score rule flag fewer of them than the IQR rule?
o: The z-score ignores large values
approxQuantile is not exact
IQR always flags more rows
The extremes inflate the mean and standard deviation, so they hide each other
e: Mean and standard deviation are pulled by extremes. Quartiles are robust: a few huge values barely move them.

q: You cap `avg_weekly_minutes` with `F.least(F.greatest(x, F.lit(lower)), F.lit(upper))`. Where should `lower` and `upper` come from?
o: `approxQuantile` on the full table
`approxQuantile` on the training split, then the same values for test and new data
`approxQuantile` on each split separately
`approxQuantile` on the test split, to match the evaluation data
e: Learned thresholds are fit on the training set only and reused unchanged, so the test set stays unseen.
